beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW - Claude UI cold open. The prompt is an ILLUSTRATIVE RECONSTRUCTION of the walker ask, never a transcript.
beats.narration_text: Mingalaba, this is Liam, in for Bear. The ask, reconstructed: Lamplight is a 2D game about a lantern that is its own light. Make three simple 3D assets for it in Blender by directing Claude through the Blender MCP, change at least one thing by hand, and show all three together in Godot at the size the game needs.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about Lamplight, a 2D platformer where Wick, a walking brass lantern, climbs out of a dark mine, into three simple 3D assets for the game: a lamp post, an oil drop and a pit prop. Build each one in my open Blender through the Blender MCP, at the game's scale, from basic shapes, then export it and show all three in a Godot 3D scene.
output: scale: 160 px = 1 m · Wick 0.35 m · tunnel 2.0 m
build: one execute_blender_code per part, read back after each
proof: Godot headless 30/0 + glb 18/0, and Rui's look

beats.role_note: What was built, with one real correction: every number matched the brief, and Rui still found the look wrong.
beats.narration_text: Three assets: a lamp post, an oil drop and a pit prop. Claude wrote every line of the Blender code, through the MCP. Rui set the scale, approved every step, made the hand edit, and, after one look in Godot, doubled the oil drop. The numbers were right. The look was not.

props.text:
Lamplight in 3D:
the look was right.

beats.role_note: The 2D game, so the viewer knows what the three assets are for.
beats.narration_text: This is the game the assets come from. Wick is a brass lantern, the oil drop refills his light, and the lamp post is where he comes back to. The game is flat, so these three are its first pieces in 3D, shown in a small room of their own.

beats.role_note: The scale the brief is written in, each number from a cited line of A2 code.
beats.narration_text: Everything starts with one conversion: one hundred sixty pixels is one metre. Wick's collider is fifty six pixels, so he is thirty five centimetres tall. A tunnel is three hundred twenty pixels, two metres. So the lamp post is seventy two and a half centimetres, copied from its pixels, and the pit prop is exactly one tunnel high.

beats.role_note: Brief-before-build evidence and the predicted failure cases.
beats.narration_text: The brief was committed and tagged before anything was built. It fixed every size to the millimetre, put every origin at the base, set a triangle budget, and predicted nine failures: lying on its side, ten times too big, floating, scale not applied, colour lost, faces missing.

beats.role_note: Interface notes (Rui's screenshot) and the MCP setup friction.
beats.narration_text: Rui learned the window first, and wrote the notes in Rui's own words. One line stuck: the default cube is two metres wide at a scale of one. Then the setup. The chapter's registration line failed as written: the dash e flag swallowed the server's name. Name first, and it connected.

shot.label: Screenshot by Rui + Claude's setup log

beats.role_note: A real prompt to Claude and what the MCP built.
beats.narration_text: Here is the loop, in Rui's real session. Rui approves a plan, and Claude builds one part per call: post, crossbar, lamp box, window, flame. Five boxes, sixty triangles. Every size is read back from the vertices, because the scene report rounds to two decimals.

shot.label: Screenshot by Rui + MCP look capture

beats.role_note: Rui's hand edit and the read-back that caught an accidental change.
beats.narration_text: Then Rui's hand edit. The flame looked a little dark, so Rui changed its base colour from amber to a pale yellow, F D F F A 6. Reading the edit back caught something else: the window glass had changed too, by accident. Rui said put it back, and it went back.

beats.role_note: Inspect-and-revise inside Blender: shape, shading, a rejected part.
beats.narration_text: The oil drop shows how a look gets argued. A round sphere at this size reads as a ball, so the body is squashed and a cone sits on it as the tip. Smooth shading exposed a seam, so the two were welded. Rui tried a highlight ball, and rejected it as ugly. Sixty four triangles.

shot.label: MCP look captures + the A2 sprite

beats.role_note: Why Apply Transforms matters, on a real unapplied state.
beats.narration_text: The pit prop, plain, read like a door frame, so Rui added two braces. Those braces sat at forty five degrees, with their scale not applied. Exported like that, Godot would get rotated, scaled nodes. Apply all transforms, and every asset leaves Blender at rotation zero, scale one, origin on the floor.
In Godot, the room is a plain scene: a floor, one light, one camera, and each asset placed at height zero. No offset, no scale. If an origin were wrong, this is where an asset would float.

beats.narration_text: The headless check measures each asset against the floor node, not against itself. A check that only measured the asset would prove nothing about the floor.

props.title: Measured against the floor.
props.source: Verbatim project source at commit 4b4b77f · Godot editor reconstruction (teaching view)
props.code:
var b := merged_aabb(node, null)
				var over_floor := b.position.x >= floor_box.position.x and b.end.x <= floor_box.end.x \
					and b.position.z >= floor_box.position.z and b.end.z <= floor_box.end.z
				# measured against the Floor node's own top, not against the asset itself
				check(asset + ".rests_on_floor", absf(b.position.y - floor_y) <= TOL and over_floor,

beats.role_note: Visible result of B12: actual recorded output, including the deliberate failures.
beats.narration_text: Headless: thirty checks, zero failures, every size within a millimetre of the brief. And each kind of check was broken on purpose, to see it fail: export without Y up, lift the drop five centimetres, keep a stale file. Each one failed.

beats.role_note: Rui's human check and the revision it caused.
beats.narration_text: Then the check no script can run. Rui walked the camera around and said: the oil drop can't be this small, and the frame is a bit too big. The drop's fifteen centimetres was the exact pixel conversion. The numbers were right; the look was not. So the drop doubled, and the frame got narrower and thinner, still two metres tall.

shot.label: Before re-rendered from 8d07135 · after from the current build

beats.role_note: Verdict: checked, uncertain, next step, contributions, source revision.
beats.narration_text: The verdict. Shown working: three assets built through the MCP, exported upright, at the brief's size, standing on the floor, with forty eight checks passing. Still uncertain: the colours render brighter than their hex values, the room is not lit like the game, and Wick is still a box. Next: light the room the way the game is lit. Claude wrote every line of Blender and Godot code. Rui chose the assets and the scale, made the hand edit, and made the call that changed two sizes.

next step — light the room the way Lamplight is lit (dark, one warm point light) and look again.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the paste ready prompt. Pick one asset from your game and write its size in metres from something the player already knows. Predict the one way it will go wrong, and the check that would catch it. Build it through the MCP, put it in Godot, and look at it beside your character before you trust the numbers. Liam, in for Bear.

Show me the numbers, then let me look before we trust them.
